title: The Ordinary Weather
premise: Zephyrine Dunmore has spent thirty years tuning pianos in other people's houses while keeping her own family's history locked inside the decaying house on Vane Street. At her mother's funeral, a stranger calls the family by their true surname—D'Anmour—and reveals that her mother spent decades hiding a wrongful conviction that destroyed another branch of the family. As Zephyrine investigates through radiators, letters, and a cousin she never knew existed, she must choose between protecting her mother's memory and telling the truth aloud. The novel ends with Zephyrine speaking the family's real name at the empty house's final viewing, then signing the sale papers, having finally said goodbye properly.
about_author: Petra Joubert is a former piano restorer from Cape Town who now writes full-time in a house with notoriously loud pipes. The Ordinary Weather is her second novel, following the acclaimed The Long Way Down the Stairs.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. She tunes a dying woman's upright piano, reading the house's grief through its heating pipes, and returns home to news of her mother's stroke. Establishes her gift for listening and her habit of deflecting intimacy. Emotional beat: quiet dread beneath practiced composure.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. At the sparsely attended funeral, a grey-haired stranger offers condolences using the name 'D'Anmour,' which Zephyrine has never heard. Her brother Marcus dismisses it as senility; Zephyrine can't let it go. Emotional beat: the first crack in the wall of invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Clearing her mother's house, she finds a radiator valve engraved D.A. and a hidden envelope of legal correspondence from 1974 concerning a man named Elias D'Anmour, convicted of arson. Emotional beat: curiosity hardening into obligation.

chapters.title: Marcus Says Sell
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Marcus. He wants the house sold quickly and the past buried, revealing he knows more than he admits. Their argument exposes old wounds about who stayed to care for their mother. Emotional beat: loyalty weaponized against truth.

chapters.title: The Stranger at the Gate
chapters.summary: Zephyrine tracks down the funeral stranger: Ruth D'Anmour, Elias's daughter, who believes Zephyrine's mother testified falsely against him. Ruth is not vengeful but exhausted, wanting only acknowledgment before she dies. Emotional beat: the weight of inherited silence.

chapters.title: Letters in the Piano Bench
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Inside the bench of her mother's own piano, she finds unsent letters in which her mother rehearses a confession she never mailed. Zephyrine learns the testimony was coerced by a landlord threatening the children. Emotional beat: grief complicated by understanding.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. A developer's offer on the house forces a deadline; Marcus signs preliminary papers. Ruth asks Zephyrine for one thing—not money, but a public statement clearing Elias's name. Emotional beat: justice revealed as something the law never delivered.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, climax. At the county archive hearing on the estate, instead of quietly consenting to the sale, Zephyrine reads her mother's final letter aloud, naming the coercion and Elias's innocence. Marcus walks out; strangers listen. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into release.

chapters.title: The Last Viewing
chapters.summary: Alternating Zephyrine and Ruth. Before closing, the sisters-in-truth walk the empty house together; Zephyrine plays the untuned piano one last time and speaks goodbye to her mother by name—the real one. Emotional beat: mourning completed at last.

chapters.title: Ordinary Weather
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, resolution. Weeks later, she tunes a piano in a bright new apartment, rain on the windows, Ruth's thank-you note on the stand. Marcus sends a terse but unbroken message. She answers the doorbell without rehearsing a smile. Emotional beat: ordinary life, finally inhabited.
